extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (general educated audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Explication of Locke's empiricist account of where ideas come from and methodological guidance for forming and evaluating knowledge — arguing against innate principles and for experience/reflection as the sources of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right use of faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: OUR KNOWLEDGE DEPENDS UPON THE RIGHT USE OF THOSE POWERS NATURE HATH BESTOWED UPON US.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One's possession of faculties is not enough; knowledge depends on how those faculties are employed. Misuse (e.g., lazy assent) deprives people of knowledge even if faculties exist. Emphasises active employment of one's powers of mind to discover, receive, and retain truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think and know for yourself (avoid blind assent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men must think and know for themselves. Do not take things upon trust or 'lazily enslave their minds to the dictates and dominion of others' but examine doctrines carefully rather than swallowing them with implicit faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer employing your own reason over accepting the opinions of revered names; borrowed opinions, however true, remain 'shreds' in your understanding unless examined. Anti-pattern: yielding assent out of reverence for authority rather than understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at truth over authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth has been my only aim; wherever that has appeared to lead, my thoughts impartially followed, without minding whether the footsteps of any other lay that way or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greatest reverence to truth rather than to authorities. In inquiry, do not shore up arguments by assuming principles from authority; base claims on candid appeal to experience and observation. Avoid accepting principles because they 'must not be questioned.'

rubrics_metrics.name: All ideas derive from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: In that all our knowledge is founded; and from that it ultimately derives itself. Our observation employed either, about external sensible objects, or about the internal operations of our minds perceived and reflected on by ourselves, is that which supplies our understandings with all the MATERIALS of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's central empiricist claim: the fountains of knowledge are sensation and reflection. This is both a descriptive claim about origins of ideas and a normative guideline for grounding knowledge in experience rather than supposing innate ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation as source of sensible ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Senses, conversant about particular sensible objects, do convey into the mind several distinct perceptions of things... and thus we come by those IDEAS we have of yellow, white, heat, cold, soft, hard, bitter, sweet, and all those which we call sensible qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify ideas of colors, tastes, textures, and other sensible qualities as arising from external objects via sensation. When assessing the source of an idea, check whether it corresponds to sensible perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection as source of ideas of mental operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The perception of the operations of our own mind within us, as it is employed about the ideas it has got;—which operations, when the soul comes to reflect on and consider, do furnish the understanding with another set of ideas... such are perception, thinking, doubting, believing, reasoning, knowing, willing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideas of mental acts and passions are produced by internal attention to one's own mental operations. To form these ideas one must reflect inwardly; they do not come from external objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustiveness: every idea is from sensation or reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The understanding seems to me not to have the least glimmering of any ideas which it doth not receive from one of these two. EXTERNAL OBJECTS furnish the mind with the ideas of sensible qualities... and THE MIND furnishes the understanding with ideas of its own operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological test: when investigating any supposed idea, try to trace it back to either sensation or reflection. This is used to reject claims of other origins (notably innate ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical appeal to observation and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: All that I shall say for the principles I proceed on is, that I can only appeal to men’s own unprejudiced experience and observation whether they be true or not; and this is enough for a man who professes no more than to lay down candidly and freely his own conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support philosophical claims by appealing to observable experience (e.g., examination of children, personal introspection). Use empirical examples rather than abstract assertions as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicion of innate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Hitherto,—to clear my way to those foundations which I conceive are the only true ones... it hath been necessary for me to give an account of the reasons I had to doubt of innate principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume universal, inborn principles exist merely because some propositions appear self-evident; their apparent universality may be due to common exposure or instruction. Anti-pattern: taking 'general propositions that could not be doubted as soon as understood' to be innate without examining their origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use developmental observation as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: He that attentively considers the state of a child, at his first coming into the world, will have little reason to think him stored with plenty of ideas... It is BY DEGREES he comes to be furnished with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the acquisition timeline of ideas (e.g., in children) to assess whether ideas are innate or acquired. Empirical developmental facts (what infants/children display) function as evidence for the origin of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention is required for reflective ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of Reflection later, because they need Attention... because, though they pass there continually, yet, like floating visions, they make not deep impressions enough to leave in their mind clear, distinct, lasting ideas, till the understanding turns inward upon itself, reflects on its own operations, and makes them the objects of its own contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To form clear, distinct ideas of mental operations one must deliberately attend to them. Lack of attentive reflection explains why many people never form such ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid construing convenience or authority as evidence of innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: When men have found some general propositions that could not be doubted of as soon as understood, it was... a short and easy way to conclude them innate. This being once received, it eased the lazy from the pains of search...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of conflating the practical or pedagogical convenience of labeling some claims 'innate' with their truth. Treat such attributions skeptically and favour inquiry and demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception and having ideas are identical
rubrics_metrics.description: To ask, at what TIME a man has first any ideas, is to ask, when he begins to perceive;—HAVING IDEAS, and PERCEPTION, being the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing consciousness or the origin of ideas, treat perception as the occurrence of ideas; use this identification in arguments about when ideas first appear (e.g., in infants).
